before.exam_tip_html: For Question 2, the examiner is looking for genuine comparison, not two separate analyses. Every sentence should reference both poems or use a comparison connective. If your paragraph does not contain words like “similarly,” “however,” “whereas,” or “in contrast,” you are probably not comparing. One well-structured PEECPEED paragraph with clear connectives, embedded quotations from both poems, and method-level analysis will comfortably reach Level 3 (7–8 marks).

When writing about Exposure, always comment on the half-rhyme — it is one of Owen’s most distinctive techniques and shows the examiner you understand form and structure. Explain that half-rhyme creates unease and dissatisfaction, mirroring the soldiers’ unresolved suffering. For Storm on the Island, don’t forget the allegorical reading — examiners reward students who can discuss the poem on both a literal and metaphorical level (the storm and the Troubles).

For the 30-mark essay on Stave 5, compare similes across staves to show structural awareness. Always link Scrooge’s actions in Stave 5 back to specific moments in Stave 1 to demonstrate understanding of the cyclical structure. Include Dickens’s social purpose — the examiner rewards answers that explain why Dickens wrote the novella, not just what happens in it. Use phrases like “Dickens intends the reader to…” or “Dickens uses this to convey his message that…”

When writing about Tissue, examiners reward students who can explain the extended metaphor clearly. Don’t just say ‘paper represents life’ — explain how different types of paper (Koran pages, maps, receipts, tissue/skin) represent different aspects of human experience. For Poppies, always discuss the mother’s perspective and her specific domestic imagery — this is what makes the poem distinctive.

When writing about The Prelude, always discuss the shift in tone (the volta). The examiner wants to see that you understand how the poem moves from beauty to terror. Use the term ‘sublime’ — it shows you understand the Romantic context. If comparing with another poem, focus on how both poets present nature as a force that overwhelms or changes human beings.
